<reason>Side A (CON) ran the cleaner path to victory. The pressure question demanding a single format whose benefits were measured before a ban forced an honest concession from B, and A exploited it relentlessly and legitimately: the "trivial or dangerous, choose one" dilemma plus the fee-dominance argument (fees fail cheaply and self-correct; bans survive on sunk costs and political momentum) gave a third-party reader a concrete reason to vote CON. A answered both of B's pressure questions directly with A1/A2 structure and kept the clash narrow. B's best material was real: the false-choice/proportionality rebuttal (a modest rule need not solve all litter to justify itself), the point that fees require the same unperformed accounting, and the sharp closing dilemma that a fee producing "the same phaseout" also imposes the same transition costs. But B's case demonstrably shrank after the concession to redundant sleeves plus promises of future justification, and B never quantified or exemplified the benefit side for any meaningful format. B's epistemic honesty (refusing to invent a study) is creditworthy but could not restore the missing evidence. Margin is kept modest because B's fee-dilemma and proportionality responses kept A's dominance argument from fully closing the door.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side A's Pressure Q1 (name one format measured before a ban) followed by A4.1's exploitation of B's concession — "the conditional is doing all the work while never being demonstrated" — was the decisive exchange, only partially blunted by B4.4's proportionality defense and B5.3's counter-dilemma that a fee achieving the same phaseout carries the same transition costs.</best_rebuttal>
